lesson.title: Emergency management that protects staff
lesson.reading: じゅうぎょういんをまもるきんきゅうかんり

objectives.text: Explain training and equipment management based on the fire plan
Judge health reporting and work adjustments
Protect yourself when dealing with suspicious objects or vomit
Explain two-direction routes and checks when one direction is unavailable
Distinguish alarm monitoring, shift handover and specialist maintenance

sections.title: Train and keep equipment ready
sections.body: Managers should review not only attendance but whether reporting, firefighting and evacuation-guidance roles were carried out. Firefighting drills practice trained initial extinguishing methods; evacuation drills practice safe movement and guiding guests; reporting drills practice internal alerts and contacting fire services. They are different activities. Connect each role, its backup, drill dates and review to the fire plan. For specified fire-prevention premises, applicable legislation may require firefighting and evacuation drills at least twice yearly; check reporting-drill frequency in the fire plan. Do not memorize an identical statutory frequency for all three. Check applicability with fire-safety personnel for the facility’s size and conditions and reflect it in the plan. Keep fire doors and evacuation routes free of luggage and do not obstruct door travel or passage. Do not assume identical equipment or inspection conditions at all facilities; alarm monitoring and maintenance are considered separately below. Keep combustible linen, paper waste and magazines away from fire and dispose of cigarette ends as instructed.

sections.title: Do not conceal symptoms based on your own judgment
sections.body: Report diarrhea, vomiting, fever, cough, sore throat or other symptoms before work and consult the responsible person about attendance and medical assessment. Report illness developing during a shift even when busy. Managers should check tasks, food contact and effects on colleagues and adjust work. Do not use the textbook’s 37.5°C figure as a universal boundary for every infection or work restriction. Symptoms still require reporting below that temperature, and return-to-work conditions must be checked against facility procedures and medical or public health instructions.

sections.title: Do not handle suspicious objects or vomit alone at risk
sections.body: When you notice a suspicious object or dangerous behavior, coordinate with the person in charge and other staff, involving police where necessary. Do not approach when your safety cannot be maintained. If vomit is found, keep people away and notify the responsible staff. Trained personnel should use gloves, a mask, gown and other required protection and avoid splashing. To prevent secondary infection such as norovirus, follow the current facility procedure and product instructions for gentle wiping, appropriate disinfection, rinsing with water, sealed disposal and handwashing afterward. Do not touch it barehanded or mix disinfectants on your own. Sodium hypochlorite is an example of a disinfectant used against norovirus. Knowing the chemical name is different from being able to prepare and use it safely. Do not use the source’s brief “disinfect before removal” sequence as an operating procedure; follow current official guidance and facility procedures. Wear protective equipment, gently wipe up waste, then proceed to disinfection of contaminated surfaces, wiping with water and sealed disposal. Contaminated surfaces and waste may need different conditions; do not memorize one concentration for every use. Confirm the target, concentration and precautions in training, including effects on materials and surroundings.

sections.title: Hand over information without unauthorized removal
sections.body: Do not copy a customer register onto a personal laptop and take it home, even to send guest information or direct mail. Use approved devices, access rights and network controls. Managers should clarify who uses information, for what purpose and how it is handled after work ends. Report suspected external transmission or loss promptly rather than handling it alone, and prevent further harm.

sections.title: Check two evacuation directions
sections.body: The Type 2 source calls for checking whether escape is possible in two directions, rather than only knowing one emergency exit. This is more than counting two exit signs. Use the facility evacuation plan and on-site checks to confirm routes from your workplace or guestrooms to safety, including what to do if one direction is unavailable. In a practice corridor diagram, suppose stairs A and B are to the left and right. If smoke is on the A side, do not lead people toward A merely because it is the usual shortcut; check the B-side route conditions and facility instructions. Drawing two arrows that immediately converge at the same dangerous place does not verify a safe alternative. Ask responsible staff how independent routes are secured in the actual building and where to guide people. This diagram and the A/B labels are learning assumptions, not a judgment of every hotel’s structure or legal design compliance. Report obstructions, doors that will not open, smoke or damage, and never guarantee an unchecked route is safe.

sections.title: Distinguish alarm monitoring from maintenance
sections.body: The source’s 24-hour monitoring and regular maintenance of fire alarms are both necessary tasks; completing one does not replace the other. Monitoring maintains continuity in who recognizes alarms and abnormalities and who receives the report, including at night and shift changes. During maintenance, designated inspectors check equipment condition, causes of faults and the need for repairs. Outgoing staff hand over unresolved fault areas, contacts already notified and interim measures. This does not mean general staff take over specialist inspection or repair. Do not first dismiss an alarm as the usual malfunction: ensure safety and follow facility procedures to check, report and guide evacuation. Do not silence it merely because it is noisy before confirming there is no fire. Report repeated faults too, including area, time, display and response, so they lead to inspection. The source’s broad wording about identical mandatory equipment does not establish identical installation and inspection conditions for all buildings. Check specific equipment and monitoring arrangements against the fire plan and applicable standards.

terms.meaning: A door intended to limit the spread of fire and smoke
Infection spreading from a source to another person
Checking escape routes in two directions, including when one is unavailable.
Assigned roles and methods that maintain continuous recognition and reporting of alarms and abnormalities across time periods and shift changes.
Inspection and necessary action to keep equipment usable.

example.situation: Before the night-to-early shift change, an alarm-equipment fault remains unresolved and a linen cart stands in front of the usual stairs. The next drill schedule says only “fire drill.”
steps: Follow facility procedures so the cart does not obstruct a door or route and check both evacuation directions.
Hand over the alarm fault’s area, time, notified contacts and response status to the early shift.
Do not substitute a specialist inspection request for ongoing monitoring.
Separate the schedule into firefighting, evacuation and reporting drills and check applicable frequencies and fire-plan roles.

practice.prompt: Draw routes A and B in a corridor diagram modeled on a facility and explain guidance when one direction is unusable. On separate sheets organize alarm-fault handover and fire-drill planning, explaining who checks what. Actual evacuation uses the facility’s verified plan.
expectedPoints: Check route conditions as well as two exit signs
Distinguish monitoring handover from specialist inspection
Separate firefighting, evacuation and reporting activities and their frequency requirements
Do not describe unresolved faults as resolved

questions.prompt: An employee with diarrhea says they can work because their temperature is below 37.5°C. What is appropriate?
choices: Decide attendance solely by temperature
Report symptoms and decide according to tasks and facility procedures
Tell them to conceal it because work is busy
Food handling is always safe
questions.explanation: Do not decide from a single temperature value. Report symptoms and work circumstances to the responsible person.

questions.prompt: What is appropriate immediately after finding vomit?
choices: Pick it up quickly with bare hands
Keep people away and contact trained staff
Vacuum it up
Mix several chemicals and spread them
questions.explanation: Protect the surrounding area and involve staff using suitable protection and procedures.

questions.prompt: Customer direct-mail work is unfinished. What is appropriate?
choices: Copy the entire register to a personal computer and take it home
Send the register to a friend for help
Consult the responsible person about work within approved systems and access rights
Transfer it to a USB drive without authorization
questions.explanation: A work purpose does not justify unauthorized removal of information.

questions.prompt: A linen cart is directly in front of a fire door. What is appropriate?
choices: Remove the obstruction according to procedures so the door can function
It is always acceptable for a short period
Add carts to hold the door in place
It is fine if guests do not see it
questions.explanation: Maintain fire-door function and unobstructed escape routes.

questions.prompt: You are checking the fire plan. How should the three drills be distinguished?
choices: Firefighting practices initial extinguishing; evacuation practices movement and guidance; reporting practices alerts and fire-service contact
All three require only attendance sheets
Reporting drills practice sales reports
Evacuation drills only require memorizing exit names
questions.explanation: Each drill practices different actions. Assign staff and backups and check actual coordination.

questions.prompt: How should drill frequencies be handled?
choices: Reporting drills are always exactly twice yearly at every facility
Check applicable firefighting/evacuation frequencies separately from the reporting frequency in the fire plan
Repeat last year without reading the plan
High attendance removes the need to check drill types
questions.explanation: Check applicable building conditions. Distinguish statutory firefighting/evacuation frequencies for specified premises from reporting frequencies set by the fire plan.

questions.prompt: In a practice corridor, routes lead left and right from guestrooms to stairs A and B. Smoke is visible toward A. What should you do?
choices: Use A because it is the usual shortcut
Two exit signs remove the need to check conditions
Check the B-side route and facility instructions and guide toward safety
Guess a route through an unfamiliar passage
questions.explanation: Checking two directions prepares for one being unavailable. Confirm actual route conditions and the facility plan, not only diagram counts.

questions.prompt: At night-to-early shift change, an alarm fault is unresolved. What should you do?
choices: Ignore alarms once handover ends
Record inspection complete if there is no sound
Erase the fault area and say nothing
Hand over area, time, notified contacts and interim measures
questions.explanation: Keep monitoring and reporting continuous and distinguish them from specialist maintenance. Hand over unresolved faults and response status.

questions.prompt: The alarm has repeatedly activated and absence of fire is unconfirmed. What is appropriate?
choices: Do not assume a malfunction; ensure safety and check and report under facility procedures
Silence and ignore it because it is routine
Independently change wiring outside your duties
Turn off power to prevent noise near guests
questions.explanation: Do not stop an alarm merely for noise before confirming no fire. Report repeated abnormalities for inspection or investigation.

choices: Paper waste may be kept near flames
Keep linen and paper away from ignition sources and dispose of cigarette ends as instructed
Mix cigarette ends into paper waste
Evacuation drills make daily checks unnecessary
questions.explanation: Drills and daily fire prevention are separate preparations. Check combustible storage and cigarette-end disposal specifically.

questions.prompt: You develop diarrhea and abdominal pain during a crowded event. What should you do?
choices: Tell no one below 37.5°C
Always continue food work until the crowd leaves
Taking medicine yourself removes reporting duties
Promptly tell a supervisor or colleague and adjust tasks and work arrangements
questions.explanation: Report illness during work as well as before shifts. Do not conceal it because of workload; follow procedures and necessary instructions.

questions.prompt: You see dangerous behavior and cannot respond safely alone. What should you do?
choices: From a safe position seek the manager and support, arranging police contact when necessary
Approach after judging someone suspicious from nationality alone
Always restrain them alone
Leave it to guests and do not report
questions.explanation: Ensure your safety and coordinate several staff based on actual behavior. Contact police when necessary.

questions.prompt: How should a worker who knows only the vomit-cleanup chemical name be instructed?
choices: Use one concentration for every target
Greater concentration removes material and precaution checks
Confirm facility procedures in training, including protection, gentle wiping and target-appropriate disinfection
Mixing chemicals makes them safe
questions.explanation: A chemical name alone is insufficient. Check protection, splash prevention, target-specific conditions and precautions and follow trained procedures.

questions.prompt: Which distinction between fire-alarm monitoring and maintenance is appropriate?
choices: Assigning monitors removes maintenance needs
General staff repair equipment independently
Repeated false alarms need only silencing
Continue monitoring while designated inspectors check equipment condition, fault causes and repair needs during maintenance
questions.explanation: Distinguish initial alarm response from regular inspection and cause checks that preserve equipment. Monitors do not take over specialist repairs.

questions.prompt: Which disinfectant does the source mention for norovirus control?
choices: Only cooking oil
Sodium hypochlorite
Sugar water
Perfume
questions.explanation: The source names sodium hypochlorite. Knowing the name differs from safe preparation and use. Check the target and current facility procedure; do not independently mix chemicals.

illustration.caption: Check two routes from guestrooms and hand over responsibilities for alarm monitoring and maintenance.
illustration.alt: A learning floor plan shows routes from guestrooms to left and right stairs, with a shift-handover diagram for fault information on the right. This is not an actual facility plan.
